title: Explore: Noop adapter policy surface
description: Inspect the disabled integration policy, capability resolution, and adapter factory to determine whether noop adapters are accidental leftovers or an explicit runtime contract.
findings: Disabled integration policy is centralized in `INTEGRATION_POLICY` and `createIntegrationAdapters`, which classify Neo4j projection, DBHub governance, and Langflow orchestration as `disabled` and intentionally instantiate explicit Noop adapters instead of advertising support.

title: Explore: Runtime behavior and call-site guards
description: Inspect the noop adapter implementations and runtime call sites to verify the actual disabled behavior and whether any critical path still depends on the interfaces remaining present.
findings: `NoopGraphProjectionAdapter` and `NoopGovernanceHookAdapter` return `false`, while `NoopOrchestrationHookAdapter` returns a disabled status object. `graph-engine.ts` guards Neo4j projection behind `flags.neo4jEnabled` and preserves the local-first path on failures, so the noop classes are compatibility boundaries rather than dead code.

title: Explore: Tests, issue history, and documentation drift
description: Inspect tests, issue history, and production-readiness docs to determine whether the repository's current truth matches the historical cleanup plan around noop adapters.
findings: Tests assert the default local-first noop contract and disabled support-level signaling, and issue `ISS-20260428-006` is already completed as implemented. The remaining gap is documentation drift: `PRODUCTION_READINESS_EXECUTION_PLAN.md` still contains early wording that says the default strategy is to remove noop adapters, while `PRODUCTION_READINESS_TODO.md` and the shipped code intentionally keep the interfaces.

title: Score: Feasibility
description: Score feasibility for bringing noop-adapter decisions fully into alignment with code, tests, and docs.
findings: Aligning the noop-adapter decision record is highly feasible because the runtime contract is already implemented and covered by tests. The remaining work is primarily decision and documentation reconciliation, not a risky code migration.
recommendations: Update the Stage 5 execution-plan wording to match the shipped retained-interface strategy, and treat any future class-removal work as a separate design change that starts with caller and type-surface refactors.

title: Score: Impact
description: Score impact of clarifying the noop-adapter contract on current-head engineering quality and downstream planning.
findings: Impact is moderate because runtime behavior is already consistent, but the clarification removes future churn risk, prevents misguided cleanup work, and keeps release-readiness narratives aligned with the actual integration contract.
recommendations: Prioritize decision consistency over more cleanup churn: document that disabled integrations remain explicit boundaries until their callers and types disappear.

title: Score: Risk
description: Score risk of the current noop-adapter state and of reopening the old removal strategy.
findings: Risk is moderate. The current runtime contract is safe, but reopening blanket noop-adapter removal without first refactoring call sites such as `graph-engine.ts` would reintroduce false assumptions and could break the local-first fallback contract.
recommendations: Do not convert this topic back into a generic class-deletion cleanup. Preserve the existing non-throwing disabled behavior and guard semantics until runtime dependencies are intentionally removed.

title: Score: Complexity
description: Score the integration complexity involved in keeping or changing the noop-adapter contract.
findings: Complexity is low-to-moderate for decision alignment and documentation cleanup, but materially higher for real adapter removal because bundle types, factory wiring, guards, and tests would all need coordinated refactors.
recommendations: Keep the near-term scope small: docs and decision alignment only. If true removal is ever needed, scope it as a separate refactor with explicit caller inventory.

title: Score: Alignment
description: Score alignment with the repository's local-first architecture and support-level policy.
findings: The current retained noop-adapter contract is strongly aligned with the repo's local-first architecture. Disabled integrations are surfaced honestly through support levels, capabilities, and deterministic fallback behavior instead of hidden half-support.
recommendations: Keep `support_level`, capability resolution, and disabled runtime signaling as the single source of truth for optional integrations.

title: Score: Maintainability
description: Score maintainability of the current noop-adapter arrangement.
findings: Maintainability is good but not perfect. The code and tests are coherent, yet historical planning language still points engineers toward class removal even though the current implementation intentionally retains explicit boundaries for disabled integrations.
recommendations: Preserve the existing regression tests, and reconcile historical docs so future work does not fork into competing interpretations of the noop contract.

title: Decision Synthesis
description: Compile the noop-adapter findings into analysis.md, context.md, and conclusions.json. Decide whether the current contract should be preserved, changed, or deferred.
findings: Current head supports a conditional go: keep the retained noop-adapter contract, do not reopen blanket class removal, and align historical Stage 5 wording with the shipped local-first disabled-integration behavior.
recommendations: Preserve disabled adapters as explicit runtime boundaries, keep the non-throwing fallback contract, and treat any future class-removal effort as a separate refactor that starts with call-site and type-surface elimination.
